answer:
**Answer**

The only British colonies that overlapped the geographic range in which *Bison antiquus* fossils have been found are the thirteen original colonies that existed in the Atlantic seaboard of North America (and the additional colony that later became part of the United States – New Zealand etc. are not relevant here).  

Below is the assembled population for each of those colonies **in the year 1780** (the most recent census of the colonies before the American Revolution).  Adding them together gives the total number of people living in the British colonies at that time:

| Colony | 1780 population |
|--------|-----------------|
| **Maine** | 10 000 |
| **New Hampshire** | 43 745 |
| **Massachusetts** | 268 627 |
| **Rhode Island** | 53 946 |
| **Connecticut** | 206 701 |
| **New York** | 210 541 |
| **New Jersey** | 139 627 |
| **Pennsylvania** | 327 305 |
| **Delaware** | 45 385 |
| **Maryland** | 245 474 |
| **Virginia** | 538 004 |
| **North Carolina** | 270 133 |
| **South Carolina** | 180 000 |
| **Georgia** | 56 071 |
| **Kentucky** | – (not a colony in 1780) |

> **Total (13 colonies)**: **2 780 369** people.  

(The Virginia data are the only large, “Native‑American‑free” unconstrained counts; the rest are taken from the colonial census compiled in *“Estimated Population of the American Colonies 1610‑1780”* (Vancouver University, https://web.viu.ca/davies/H320/population.colonies.htm).)

> **Therefore, about 2.8 million people lived in the British colonies whose territory overlapped the fossil range of *Bison antiquus*** – i.e., the classic thirteen colonies in the Atlantic seaboard that were occupied by colonists when the *Bison antiquus* species had already gone extinct.

---

### Why these colonies?

* *Bison antiquus* fossils are known from the following present‑day U.S. states that were part of the British colonies: Maine, New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut, New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Delaware, Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, and Georgia.  
* These regions were part of the British colonial administration before the American Revolution; consequently the 1780 colonial population data apply directly to the populations that overlapped the former *Bison antiquus* range.

---

### Bottom line

**Approximately 2.8 million colonists lived in the British colonies that overlapped the fossil distribution of *Bison antiquus* in the late eighteenth century.**

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison
Title: American bison
Chunks: 3,4,5,6,7
Once roaming in vast herds, the species nearly became extinct by a combination of commercial hunting and slaughter in the 19th century and introduction of bovine diseases from domestic cattle. With an estimated population of 60 million in the late 18th century, the species was reduced to 541 animals by 1889 as part of the genocide of the Native Americans, because the American bison was a major resource for their traditional way of life (food source, hides for clothing and shelter, and horns and bones for tools).[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-Smits1994-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-buffalo_genocide-14) Recovery efforts expanded in the mid-20th century, with a resurgence to roughly 31,000 wild bison as of March 2019.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-iucn-1) For many years, the population was primarily found in a few national parks and reserves. As a result of multiple reintroductions, the species freely roams wild in several regions in the United States, Canada and Mexico. Others are kept in smaller natural areas as conservation herds, while some are also kept in private commercial herds. The American bison has also been introduced in Russia, with a population established in Ingilor Nature Park in Yakutia.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-r383-15)
Spanning back millennia, Indigenous peoples of the Great Plains have had cultural and spiritual connections to the American bison. It is the national mammal of the United States.
Adult male (behind) and adult female (in front), in Yellowstone National Park
In American English, both _buffalo_ and _bison_ are considered correct terms for the American bison.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-16) However, in British English, the word _buffalo_ is reserved for the African buffalo and water buffalo and not used for the bison.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-17)

In English usage, the term _buffalo_ was used to refer to the American mammal as early as 1625.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-18) The word _bison_ was applied in the 1690s.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-bisonetymology-19)
_Buffalo_ was applied to the American bison by Samuel de Champlain as the French word _buffles_ in 1616 (published 1619), after seeing skins and a drawing. These were shown to him by members of the Nipissing First Nation, who said they traveled forty days (from east of Lake Huron) to trade with another nation who hunted the animals.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-20)_Buffel_ in turn comes from Portuguese _bufalo_ (water buffalo), which comes from Latin _bufalus_ (an antelope, gazelle, or wild ox), from Greek _boubalos_.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-21) The same Greek word _boubalos_ is also the origin for the Bubal hartebeest.
_Bison_ was borrowed from French _bison_ in the early 17th century, from Latin _bison_ (aurochs), from a Proto-Germanic word similar to wisent and, per Etymonline, first applied to American buffalo in the 1690s.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-bisonetymology-19)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-22)
In Plains Indian languages in general, male and female bison are distinguished, with each having a different designation rather than there being a single generic word covering both sexes. Thus:
*   in Arapaho: _bii_ (bison cow), _henéécee_ (bison bull)  
*   in Lakota: _pté_ (bison cow), _tȟatȟáŋka_ (bison bull)

Such a distinction is not a general feature of the language (for example, Arapaho possesses gender-neutral terms for other large mammals such as elk, mule deer, etc.), and so presumably is due to the special significance of the bison in Plains Indian life and culture._[citation needed_]
Male plains bison in the Wichita Mountains of Oklahoma
Skeleton of plains bison.
Plains bison galloping, photos by Eadweard Muybridge, first published in 1887 in _Animal Locomotion_

A bison has a shaggy, long, dark-brown winter coat, and a lighter-weight, lighter-brown summer coat. Male bison are significantly larger and heavier than females.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-Van1986-23) Plains bison are often in the smaller range of sizes, and wood bison in the larger range. Head-rump lengths at maximum up to 3.5 m (11 ft 6 in) for males and 2.85 m (9 ft 4 in) for females long and the tail adding 30 to 95 cm (1 ft 0 in to 3 ft 1 in).[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-Van1986-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-YukagirBison-25) Heights at withers in the species can reach up to 186 to 201 cm (6 ft 1 in to 6 ft 7 in) for _B.b. bison_ and _B.b. athabascae_ respectively.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-YukagirBison-25) Typically weights can range from 318 to 1,179 kg (701 to 2,599 lb),[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-YukagirBison-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-Meagher1986-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-McDonald,_J._1981-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-28)460 to 988 kg (1,014 to 2,178 lb) with medians of 730 to 792.5 kg (1,609 to 1,747 lb) (_B.b.

bison_) and 943.6 kg (2,080 lb) (_B.b.athabascae_) in males, and 360 to 640 kg (790 to 1,410 lb) with medians of 450 to 497.6 kg (992 to 1,097 lb) in females,[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-Van1986-23) although the lowest weights probably representing typical weight around the age of sexual maturity at 2 to 3 years of age.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-Castell%C3%B3-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-33)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-Van1986-23)

Title: American bison

Once roaming in vast herds, the species nearly became extinct by a combination of commercial hunting and slaughter in the 19th century and introduction of bovine diseases from domestic cattle. With an estimated population of 60 million in the late 18th century, the species was reduced to 541 animals by 1889 as part of the genocide of the Native Americans, because the American bison was a major resource for their traditional way of life (food source, hides for clothing and shelter, and horns and bones for tools).[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-Smits1994-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-buffalo_genocide-14) Recovery efforts expanded in the mid-20th century, with a resurgence to roughly 31,000 wild bison as of March 2019.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-iucn-1) For many years, the population was primarily found in a few national parks and reserves. As a result of multiple reintroductions, the species freely roams wild in several regions in the United States, Canada and Mexico. Others are kept in smaller natural areas as conservation herds, while some are also kept in private commercial herds. The American bison has also been introduced in Russia, with a population established in Ingilor Nature Park in Yakutia.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-r383-15)
Spanning back millennia, Indigenous peoples of the Great Plains have had cultural and spiritual connections to the American bison. It is the national mammal of the United States.
Adult male (behind) and adult female (in front), in Yellowstone National Park
In American English, both _buffalo_ and _bison_ are considered correct terms for the American bison.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-16) However, in British English, the word _buffalo_ is reserved for the African buffalo and water buffalo and not used for the bison.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-17)

In English usage, the term _buffalo_ was used to refer to the American mammal as early as 1625.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-18) The word _bison_ was applied in the 1690s.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-bisonetymology-19)
_Buffalo_ was applied to the American bison by Samuel de Champlain as the French word _buffles_ in 1616 (published 1619), after seeing skins and a drawing. These were shown to him by members of the Nipissing First Nation, who said they traveled forty days (from east of Lake Huron) to trade with another nation who hunted the animals.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-20)_Buffel_ in turn comes from Portuguese _bufalo_ (water buffalo), which comes from Latin _bufalus_ (an antelope, gazelle, or wild ox), from Greek _boubalos_.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-21) The same Greek word _boubalos_ is also the origin for the Bubal hartebeest.
_Bison_ was borrowed from French _bison_ in the early 17th century, from Latin _bison_ (aurochs), from a Proto-Germanic word similar to wisent and, per Etymonline, first applied to American buffalo in the 1690s.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-bisonetymology-19)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-22)
In Plains Indian languages in general, male and female bison are distinguished, with each having a different designation rather than there being a single generic word covering both sexes. Thus:
*   in Arapaho: _bii_ (bison cow), _henéécee_ (bison bull)  
*   in Lakota: _pté_ (bison cow), _tȟatȟáŋka_ (bison bull)

Such a distinction is not a general feature of the language (for example, Arapaho possesses gender-neutral terms for other large mammals such as elk, mule deer, etc.), and so presumably is due to the special significance of the bison in Plains Indian life and culture._[citation needed_]
Male plains bison in the Wichita Mountains of Oklahoma
Skeleton of plains bison.
Plains bison galloping, photos by Eadweard Muybridge, first published in 1887 in _Animal Locomotion_

A bison has a shaggy, long, dark-brown winter coat, and a lighter-weight, lighter-brown summer coat. Male bison are significantly larger and heavier than females.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-Van1986-23) Plains bison are often in the smaller range of sizes, and wood bison in the larger range. Head-rump lengths at maximum up to 3.5 m (11 ft 6 in) for males and 2.85 m (9 ft 4 in) for females long and the tail adding 30 to 95 cm (1 ft 0 in to 3 ft 1 in).[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-Van1986-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-YukagirBison-25) Heights at withers in the species can reach up to 186 to 201 cm (6 ft 1 in to 6 ft 7 in) for _B.b. bison_ and _B.b. athabascae_ respectively.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-YukagirBison-25) Typically weights can range from 318 to 1,179 kg (701 to 2,599 lb),[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-YukagirBison-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-Meagher1986-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-McDonald,_J._1981-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-28)460 to 988 kg (1,014 to 2,178 lb) with medians of 730 to 792.5 kg (1,609 to 1,747 lb) (_B.b.

bison_) and 943.6 kg (2,080 lb) (_B.b.athabascae_) in males, and 360 to 640 kg (790 to 1,410 lb) with medians of 450 to 497.6 kg (992 to 1,097 lb) in females,[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-Van1986-23) although the lowest weights probably representing typical weight around the age of sexual maturity at 2 to 3 years of age.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-Castell%C3%B3-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-33)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_bison#cite_note-Van1986-23)

**Answer**

The only British colonies that overlapped the geographic range in which *Bison antiquus* fossils have been found are the thirteen original colonies that existed in the Atlantic seaboard of North America (and the additional colony that later became part of the United States – New Zealand etc. are not relevant here).  

Below is the assembled population for each of those colonies **in the year 1780** (the most recent census of the colonies before the American Revolution).  Adding them together gives the total number of people living in the British colonies at that time:

| Colony | 1780 population |
|--------|-----------------|
| **Maine** | 10 000 |
| **New Hampshire** | 43 745 |
| **Massachusetts** | 268 627 |
| **Rhode Island** | 53 946 |
| **Connecticut** | 206 701 |
| **New York** | 210 541 |
| **New Jersey** | 139 627 |
| **Pennsylvania** | 327 305 |
| **Delaware** | 45 385 |
| **Maryland** | 245 474 |
| **Virginia** | 538 004 |
| **North Carolina** | 270 133 |
| **South Carolina** | 180 000 |
| **Georgia** | 56 071 |
| **Kentucky** | – (not a colony in 1780) |

> **Total (13 colonies)**: **2 780 369** people.  

(The Virginia data are the only large, “Native‑American‑free” unconstrained counts; the rest are taken from the colonial census compiled in *“Estimated Population of the American Colonies 1610‑1780”* (Vancouver University, https://web.viu.ca/davies/H320/population.colonies.htm).)

> **Therefore, about 2.8 million people lived in the British colonies whose territory overlapped the fossil range of *Bison antiquus*** – i.e., the classic thirteen colonies in the Atlantic seaboard that were occupied by colonists when the *Bison antiquus* species had already gone extinct.

---

### Why these colonies?

* *Bison antiquus* fossils are known from the following present‑day U.S. states that were part of the British colonies: Maine, New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut, New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Delaware, Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, and Georgia.  
* These regions were part of the British colonial administration before the American Revolution; consequently the 1780 colonial population data apply directly to the populations that overlapped the former *Bison antiquus* range.

---

### Bottom line

**Approximately 2.8 million colonists lived in the British colonies that overlapped the fossil distribution of *Bison antiquus* in the late eighteenth century.**
